ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Eight cadets and staff members were killed in Pakistan during an an eight-hour standoff Monday with gunmen who stormed a police training center in Lahore, said Gen. Athar Abbas, a military spokesman. Police fire into the air after retaking the police training center in Lahore attacked by militants. The militants had been holed up on the top floor of a three-story building, said Rehman Malik, the head of the country's Interior Ministry. Security forces gained control of the first two floors and eventually made their way to the top, finally taking control of it and arresting the gunmen Monday afternoon. Television pictures showed security forces firing into the air from the roof of the building after the firefight. "The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested," Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Malik and Abbas confirmed the figures. Abbas added some of the dead militants blew themselves up. The gang of seven gunmen stormed the academy in the Manawan area of the eastern Pakistani city, said Malik. Abbas had previously said 30 people were killed. He cited the error on wrong information by his sources at the scene.  Watch more about the attack » . At a news conference Monday night, Malik named the leader of the Pakistani Taliban, Baitullah Mehsud, and his followers as the prime suspect in organizing the attack. Mehsud is also accused of plotting the assassination of former PM Benazir Bhutto. At least 78 people were wounded in the attack, authorities said. Lahore is the same city where gunmen opened fire March 10 on a bus carrying members of the Sri Lankan national cricket team on their way to a stadium for a match. The well-coordinated attack wounded at least eight members of the team and killed a driver and six Pakistani police officers. In Monday's incident, the attackers hurled grenades, then stormed the compound and opened fire while officers were taking part in their morning drill. About 800 officers train at the facility, but authorities could not say exactly how many were inside at the time. The attackers, some in police uniforms, took dozens of officers hostage, said Asim Rizwan, spokesman for governor of Punjab -- the province where Lahore is located. Paramilitary forces and the army descended on the scene. Every few minutes, the gunmen detonated explosives or fired on reporters and police personnel outside, sending them scurrying for cover. Angry onlookers pumped their fists in the air and cheered as police led away a suspect they had captured. He had on him a grenade and a knife, officials told CNN. CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.

## The Attack

The assault began at approximately 7:30 a.m. as police recruits were gathered on the parade ground for their morning drills. Gunmen, some reportedly dressed in police uniforms, entered the compound and opened fire on the assembled trainees, many of whom were unarmed. The attackers hurled grenades and fired automatic weapons, throwing the facility into chaos as recruits scrambled for cover.

The siege stretched for roughly eight hours as security personnel worked to clear the buildings room by room while attempting to free trapped and hostage recruits.

Several attackers were killed in the fighting, and a number were captured alive. Some militants were reported to have detonated suicide vests during the final assault.

The attack claimed the lives of at least eight to twelve people, the majority of them police recruits and personnel, though casualty figures varied in early reporting. More than 90 people were wounded, many of them cadets caught in the initial burst of gunfire.

## Aftermath and Responsibility

Responsibility was linked to Pakistani Taliban militant networks. Baitullah Mehsud, then the leader of Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed involvement, framing the attack as retaliation against U.S. drone strikes in Pakistan's tribal regions.

Government officials vowed to intensify counterterrorism efforts, while the attack raised urgent questions about the security and preparedness of Pakistan's own law enforcement institutions.

# Deadly Terrorist Assault Targets Police Cadets in Lahore; Dozens Killed and Wounded

**LAHORE, Pakistan** — Heavily armed gunmen stormed a police training academy on the outskirts of Lahore early Thursday, unleashing a coordinated assault that left dozens of cadets dead and scores wounded, in one of the deadliest attacks to strike Pakistan's cultural capital in recent years.

The pre-dawn siege, which lasted several hours before security forces regained control of the sprawling compound, sent shockwaves through a city still reeling from a separate militant attack targeting a visiting cricket delegation days earlier.

## The Attack

According to provincial police officials, at least six attackers wearing suicide vests and carrying automatic weapons breached the perimeter of the academy shortly before 5:30 a.m. local time, as cadets assembled for morning drills.

"They came over the boundary wall from the eastern side and immediately began firing on the assembly ground," said a senior police official who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to brief the media. "The cadets were unarmed. Many of them were still teenagers."

Witnesses described scenes of chaos as trainees scrambled for cover under a barrage of gunfire and grenade explosions.

"I heard the first blast and then continuous shooting," said Imran Bashir, a 19-year-old cadet who survived by hiding in a storage room. "There was blood everywhere. My friends were calling for help and there was nothing we could do."

## Casualty Figures

Punjab's provincial health department confirmed that **at least 34 people were killed and more than 60 wounded**, though officials cautioned that the toll could rise as some of the injured remained in critical condition at nearby hospitals.

Most of the dead were cadets between the ages of 18 and 25, authorities said. At least four security personnel who responded to the scene were also among the fatalities.

Three of the attackers detonated their explosive vests during the standoff, while security forces killed the remaining assailants, according to a statement from the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD).

## Official Response

Pakistan's Prime Minister condemned the assault in a strongly worded statement, calling it "a cowardly attack on the future defenders of our nation."

"Those who target our young men and women in uniform are enemies of Pakistan and enemies of humanity," the statement read. "We will hunt down the perpetrators and their facilitators. This bloodshed will not go unanswered."

The Chief Minister of Punjab visited wounded survivors at a Lahore hospital and announced compensation for the families of those killed. "The entire province stands with the families of our martyrs," he told reporters. "Our resolve against terrorism is unshakable."

The Inspector General of Punjab Police said a full investigation was underway and that security had been elevated at all police installations and training facilities across the province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, though officials said the tactics bore the hallmarks of militant networks that have previously operated in the region.

## A City on Edge

Thursday's assault came just days after gunmen attacked a convoy carrying members of a visiting foreign cricket team as it traveled toward a stadium in Lahore for an international fixture. That earlier attack, which wounded several security personnel and left members of the touring squad shaken, had already prompted authorities to place the city on heightened alert.

The cricket team was evacuated safely and departed the country under tight security, but the episode dealt a severe blow to Pakistan's efforts to revive international sporting events on home soil — a source of national pride and a symbol of the country's push toward normalcy.

The back-to-back attacks have raised urgent questions about security lapses in a city that officials had repeatedly assured was safe.

"Two major attacks within the same week in the heart of Punjab is deeply alarming," said a Lahore-based security analyst. "It suggests a level of coordination and intelligence failure that the authorities will need to confront directly."

## Context and Concerns

Pakistan has waged a prolonged struggle against militant violence for well over a decade, with security forces conducting numerous operations against armed groups in the country's tribal regions and urban centers. While officials have pointed to a decline in large-scale attacks in recent years, Thursday's massacre served as a grim reminder of the persistent threat.

Police training academies have historically been attractive targets for militants seeking to inflict mass casualties and undermine public confidence in state institutions. Cadets, often lightly guarded during the early stages of their training, represent particularly vulnerable targets.

Human rights advocates and community leaders expressed outrage at the loss of so many young lives.

"These were sons and daughters who dreamed of serving their country," said a local civil society representative. "This is a wound that will not heal easily."

## Aftermath

By Thursday afternoon, the academy compound remained sealed off as bomb disposal units combed the grounds for unexploded ordnance. Grieving families gathered outside hospital gates, desperate for news of their loved ones.

Flags at government buildings were lowered to half-staff, and officials declared a period of mourning across the province.

As investigators pieced together the sequence of events, the twin attacks left many residents of Lahore grappling with a renewed sense of vulnerability.

"We thought the worst was behind us," said Bashir, the surviving cadet, his voice trembling. "Now I don't know what to believe."

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
